title: Camus and the Absurd
subtitle: When the world will not answer, how should we live?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what Camus meant by the absurd and why it is a relationship rather than a feature of the world.
By the end you will be able to describe the three responses to the absurd in *The Myth of Sisyphus*: physical suicide, philosophical suicide and revolt.
By the end you will be able to explain why Camus concludes that one must imagine Sisyphus happy.
By the end you will be able to connect *The Stranger*, *The Plague* and *The Rebel* to Camus's philosophy.
By the end you will be able to explain Camus's quarrel with Sartre and assess criticisms of his thought.
hook:
You wake up. You catch the bus. Four hours of work, lunch, four more hours of work, dinner, sleep. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, the same rhythm. Most of the time this is fine. Then one day, perhaps on an ordinary afternoon, a small question slips in: *why?* Why all this? And suddenly the familiar scenery of your life looks like a stage set that has started to collapse.

Albert Camus described exactly this moment in *The Myth of Sisyphus* (1942). He thought it was where real philosophy begins. His book opens with one of the most startling first sentences in philosophy: there is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide. Judging whether life is or is not worth living, he says, is answering the fundamental question of philosophy. That sounds grim. But Camus's answer turns out to be a passionate *yes* to life, in a world that offers no guarantees. (If these questions ever feel personal and heavy rather than philosophical, please talk to someone you trust or contact a local crisis line. Camus himself would insist that life is worth living.)

sections.heading: A Child of the Algerian Sun
sections.body:
Albert Camus (1913–1960) came from a world very different from the Paris salons of Sartre and Beauvoir. He was born on 7 November 1913 in Mondovi, in French Algeria, to a poor family of European settlers. His father, Lucien, was killed in the First World War at the Battle of the Marne in 1914, when Albert was less than a year old. His mother, partly deaf and unable to read, cleaned houses, and the family lived in a cramped apartment in the working-class Belcourt district of Algiers, without electricity or running water.

A primary school teacher, Louis Germain, spotted the boy's talent and coached him for a scholarship to the lycée. Camus never forgot it: when he won the Nobel Prize, he wrote to Germain to thank him. As a teenager Camus played as goalkeeper for a junior side of the Racing Universitaire d'Alger football club, until at seventeen he was diagnosed with tuberculosis, a disease that would shadow him for the rest of his life.

He studied philosophy at the University of Algiers, writing a thesis on Neoplatonism and Christian thought, with Plotinus and Augustine at its centre (remember Days 28 and 30). He worked as a journalist, exposing the misery of the Kabyle region of Algeria, and ran a theatre company. During the Second World War he moved to France and became editor of *Combat*, an underground Resistance newspaper.

His three great works on the absurd appeared during the war: the novel *The Stranger* (1942), the essay *The Myth of Sisyphus* (1942) and the play *Caligula* (first performed 1945). *The Plague* (1947), *The Rebel* (1951) and *The Fall* (1956) followed. In 1957, aged 44, he received the Nobel Prize in Literature, one of the youngest laureates ever. On 4 January 1960 he died in a car crash near Villeblevin, in Burgundy; his publisher's nephew, Michel Gallimard, was driving. He was 46.

Camus was often called an existentialist, but he rejected the label. He thought of himself as a writer and moralist, and his philosophy grows less from Husserl and Heidegger than from the Mediterranean sun, poverty and a love of life's physical joys: swimming, football, the sea.

sections.heading: What Is the Absurd?
sections.body:
Camus's key concept is **the absurd**. In ordinary speech, absurd means silly or ridiculous. Camus uses it in a more precise way.

Human beings long for clarity, unity and meaning. We want to understand the world, to know why we are here and what it is all for. We want, as Camus says, the world to be reasonable. But the world does not answer. Science describes how things work, yet it cannot tell us why they matter. The universe is silent and indifferent. The absurd is born from this **confrontation** between the human call for meaning and the unreasonable silence of the world.

This point is easy to miss: for Camus, the world is not absurd in itself, and neither are humans. The absurd is a *relationship*, a divorce between a mind that demands meaning and a world that will not provide it. Remove either side, and the absurd vanishes. A stone does not feel it; neither would a god who understood everything.

How do we discover it? Sometimes through the weariness of routine, as in the hook. Sometimes through the realisation that time is carrying us toward death; we say *tomorrow* and *later* while every day brings us closer to the end. Sometimes through sudden strangeness: a familiar landscape or a face we love becomes opaque and alien. Camus has a memorable image: a man talking on the telephone behind a glass partition. You cannot hear him, you only see his pointless gestures, and you wonder why he is alive.

Notice how this differs from Nietzsche's nihilism (Day 65). Nietzsche announced that the highest values had devalued themselves and called for new values. Camus begins from the same godless world, but his question is less about creating values than about how to live honestly in the absence of final answers.

sections.heading: Three Responses: Suicide, the Leap and Revolt
sections.body:
Once we recognise the absurd, what should we do? Camus considers three answers.

**Physical suicide.** If life has no ultimate meaning, why live? Camus rejects this. Suicide does not resolve the absurd; it abolishes it by destroying one of its two terms, the human being who asks. It is a kind of surrender, a confession that life is too much. The absurd requires that we keep both sides alive: our hunger for meaning and the world's silence.

**Philosophical suicide.** The second escape is subtler. Many thinkers, Camus argues, recognise the absurd and then leap beyond it into a hope that cancels it. He discusses existentialist thinkers such as Kierkegaard (Day 64), Karl Jaspers and Lev Shestov. Kierkegaard sees that reason cannot make sense of existence and then makes a leap of faith into God, turning the very absurdity of the world into a sign of the divine. Camus respects the honesty of their starting point but calls their conclusion **philosophical suicide**: killing the mind's lucidity in exchange for a comforting answer it cannot justify. He even accuses Husserl's phenomenology (Day 75) of a similar flight toward eternal essences. He does not claim to have proved that God does not exist; his claim is that he cannot know, and he refuses to pretend.

**Revolt.** Camus's own answer is to live with the absurd, eyes open. He draws three consequences:

1. **Revolt**: a constant, lucid refusal either to give in or to accept false hope. Revolt is not rebellion against a particular tyrant here, but a defiant stance toward a meaningless fate.
2. **Freedom**: without eternal rules or a future life to earn, I am free from the illusions that once governed my behaviour. Camus is careful: this is not metaphysical free will, but the freedom of someone who no longer lives for tomorrow's rewards.
3. **Passion**: since there is no guaranteed meaning in depth, the goal becomes to live as fully as possible, to multiply experiences and savour the present with intensity.

Camus illustrates absurd lives with figures such as Don Juan the seducer, the actor who lives many lives on stage, the conqueror, and above all the artist, who creates knowing that no work lasts forever.

sections.heading: One Must Imagine Sisyphus Happy
sections.body:
The book ends with the myth that gives it its name. In Greek mythology, Sisyphus, a king of Corinth, offended the gods; stories vary about how, including tricking Death itself. His punishment in the underworld was to roll a huge boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down every time, forever. The gods, Camus says, thought there was no more dreadful punishment than futile and hopeless labour.

Sisyphus is the **absurd hero**. His life is the human condition magnified: effort without final result, repeated without end. But Camus asks us to look at Sisyphus at a particular moment, as he walks back down the hill toward his boulder. That pause is the hour of consciousness. Sisyphus knows the full extent of his wretched fate. He has no hope. And yet, precisely because he is lucid, his fate belongs to him. In Camus's words, there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.

More than that: Camus suggests that the struggle itself can be enough. The boulder is his thing, the mountain his world. The book's final sentence has become one of the most quoted lines in modern philosophy: one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

This is not the happiness of someone who has found a hidden purpose. Nothing about the boulder changes. It is the happiness of someone who has stopped waiting for the gods to explain themselves, and who finds joy in the effort, the sun, the stone and the next step. Compare the Stoics (Days 25–26), who also counselled accepting what we cannot control, and Nietzsche's *amor fati* and eternal recurrence (Day 66): could you will this life again and again? Camus's Sisyphus says yes, without consolation.

sections.heading: The Stranger and The Plague
sections.body:
Camus put his ideas into novels that reached far more readers than his essays.

*The Stranger* (1942) opens with famously flat sentences: Meursault's mother has died today, or maybe yesterday; he does not know. Meursault, a French clerk in Algiers, does not cry at the funeral. The next day he goes swimming, begins an affair and watches a comic film. Later, on a blinding hot beach, he shoots an Arab man, who is never named. At his trial the prosecution dwells less on the killing than on his failure to grieve, and he is sentenced to death. Awaiting execution, he angrily rejects a priest's consolations and opens himself to what he calls the gentle indifference of the world.

In a later preface Camus summed up his hero provocatively: in our society, any man who does not weep at his mother's funeral runs the risk of being condemned to death. Meursault refuses to lie, to say more than he feels. Society punishes him for not playing the game. Readers disagree about whether he is an absurd hero, an empty man, or something more disturbing. Postcolonial critics, including Edward Said, pointed out that the murdered Arab has no name, no voice and no story. In 2013 the Algerian writer Kamel Daoud answered with *The Meursault Investigation*, narrated by the dead man's brother, who finally names him Musa.

*The Plague* (1947) tells of an epidemic that seals off the Algerian city of Oran. Doctor Rieux fights the disease without illusions and without heroics, because it is his job and because people are suffering. Many readers took the plague as an allegory of the Nazi occupation, and of evil generally. The novel shows Camus moving from solitary revolt toward **solidarity**: the absurd is shared, and so the response to it must be shared. Rieux says that the only way to fight the plague is with decency, which he describes simply as doing his job.

sections.heading: The Rebel and the Quarrel with Sartre
sections.body:
In *The Rebel* (1951), Camus turned from suicide to murder. The question of the twentieth century, he thought, was how ideals had led to mass killing in the name of history, revolution or the future. A rebel, he argued, is a person who says no, like a slave who finally refuses an order. But in saying no, the rebel also says yes: yes to a limit, to a value shared by all human beings that the master has violated. Rebellion therefore discovers human solidarity. Camus's famous formula reworks Descartes (Day 43): I rebel, therefore we exist.

True rebellion, therefore, respects limits. It turns into tyranny when it becomes **revolution** that claims history justifies any means, sacrificing living people for a future utopia. Camus traced this logic through the French Revolution, Hegel and Marx to the Soviet labour camps. He defended instead a politics of measure and limits, which he associated with Mediterranean thought.

This was a direct challenge to the left-wing intellectuals of Paris, many of whom defended the Soviet Union as the hope of the working class. In 1952 Sartre's journal *Les Temps modernes* published a harsh review of *The Rebel* by Francis Jeanson. Camus replied angrily, addressing Sartre as the editor, and Sartre answered with a famously cutting public letter. Their friendship ended. For decades Sartre seemed the winner; after the opening of Soviet archives, many judged that Camus had been right about the camps.

Camus's position on Algeria was painful. He condemned French colonial injustice and wrote early reports on Algerian poverty, but he opposed independence as the National Liberation Front pursued it, hoped for a federal solution in which Arabs and Europeans would live as equals, and condemned terrorism and torture on both sides. A remark he made to a student in Stockholm in 1957 is reported in several versions; its gist was that if justice meant bombs that could kill his mother, he would choose his mother. Critics saw this as a settler's blindness; admirers see it as a refusal to justify killing innocents.

Other objections: philosophers find *The Myth of Sisyphus* more lyrical than rigorous; Sartre thought Camus avoided the hard choices of politics; and some ask whether revolt and solidarity can be grounded in a world he calls meaningless. Camus's answer was never a system. It was a stance: lucid, defiant and generous.

keyQuote.source: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), final sentence (Justin O'Brien translation)

modernConnection.title: Pushing the Boulder: Burnout, Bullshit Jobs and the Plague Years
modernConnection.body:
Camus's rolling boulder may be the most precise image ever made of modern working life. Many people describe their days as repetitive tasks that are undone as soon as they are finished: emptying the inbox that refills overnight, restocking shelves that will be emptied tomorrow, meeting targets that reset each quarter. The anthropologist David Graeber's *Bullshit Jobs* (2018) argued that many workers privately believe their jobs are pointless. Surveys about burnout and disengagement suggest that the hook's question, *why?*, is being asked in offices everywhere.

Popular culture has noticed. Online, Sisyphus memes and slogans about imagining Sisyphus happy circulate widely, sometimes as ironic comfort for a dreary workday. In 2020, as COVID-19 spread, sales of *The Plague* rose sharply in several countries, as readers recognised quarantine, denial, statistics and exhausted doctors in Camus's Oran. Rieux's quiet ethic of decency, just doing one's job to protect others, resonated with healthcare workers.

Camus offers something more interesting than either motivational optimism or despair. He does not promise that your work secretly matters in a cosmic plan. He suggests that meaning may be found in lucid engagement itself, and in solidarity with those pushing their own boulders beside you.

But the comparison has limits, and Camus would insist on them. Sisyphus cannot change his punishment; workers often can, through organising, changing jobs or reforming institutions. Telling an exploited worker to imagine himself happy could become exactly the false consolation Camus despised, a way of excusing injustice. *The Rebel* is clear that revolt also means saying no to unnecessary suffering imposed by other people. And clinical burnout or depression is not a philosophical stance; it calls for rest, support and sometimes treatment, not just a change of attitude. Camus's real lesson is double: accept what truly cannot be changed without lying to yourself, and refuse what can.

vocabulary.definition: Camus's term for the confrontation between the human longing for meaning and clarity and the silent, indifferent world that does not provide it.
vocabulary.example: Asking why you go to work every day and finding no ultimate answer is a first encounter with the absurd.

vocabulary.definition: Camus's name for escaping the absurd by leaping into a hope or system, such as religious faith, that the mind cannot justify, thereby giving up lucidity.
vocabulary.example: Camus accused Kierkegaard of philosophical suicide for leaping from the absurd to faith in God.

vocabulary.definition: In *The Myth of Sisyphus*, the lucid, ongoing refusal either to give in to the absurd or to deny it with false hope; in *The Rebel*, the act of saying no to injustice in the name of a shared human value.
vocabulary.example: Continuing to live passionately while admitting that the universe offers no guarantees is Camus's revolt.

vocabulary.definition: A figure who fully recognises the absurd and lives with it lucidly and passionately, without hope of escape; Sisyphus is the model.
vocabulary.example: Doctor Rieux, fighting a plague he cannot finally defeat, behaves like an absurd hero.

vocabulary.definition: Clear-eyed awareness of one's real condition, without illusions or comforting myths; for Camus, a central virtue.
vocabulary.example: Sisyphus's lucidity on his walk down the hill is what turns his punishment into his own fate.

vocabulary.definition: The bond among human beings who share the same condition and resist suffering together, central to *The Plague* and *The Rebel*.
vocabulary.example: Volunteers helping strangers during an epidemic show Camus's solidarity.

vocabulary.definition: In *The Rebel*, the protest of human beings against their condition and against creation itself, as distinct from historical rebellion against particular rulers.
vocabulary.example: Ivan Karamazov's refusal to accept a world in which children suffer is, for Camus, metaphysical rebellion.

thinkingExercise.title: Your Boulder
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use Camus's analysis to examine one repetitive part of your own life, and decide what revolt would mean there.
steps: Identify one boulder in your life: a routine or task that repeats endlessly and never feels finished.
Describe a moment when you asked *why?* about it. What answers did you try, and did any of them feel like a leap rather than an honest answer?
Separate what cannot be changed about this boulder from what could be changed through your own action or with others.
Write a short paragraph imagining yourself on the walk down the hill: what in this activity, if anything, could you find worth doing for its own sake?
Finally, judge Camus: is imagining Sisyphus happy wisdom, or a way of making peace with things we should fight?

summary: Albert Camus (1913–1960), born into poverty in French Algeria, became a novelist, journalist, Resistance editor and Nobel laureate; he rejected the label existentialist.
The absurd is not a property of the world but the confrontation between our demand for meaning and the world's silence.
In *The Myth of Sisyphus* he rejects physical suicide and philosophical suicide (the leap into hope) in favour of revolt, freedom and passion.
Sisyphus, lucid about his endless task, is the absurd hero: one must imagine Sisyphus happy.
*The Stranger* and *The Plague* dramatise the absurd and the turn toward solidarity; *The Rebel* argues that true rebellion respects limits and rejects murder justified by history.
His break with Sartre in 1952, his stance on Algeria, and the question of how to ground values in a meaningless world remain debated.

quiz.question: According to Camus, where is the absurd located?
options: In the world, which is irrational in itself
In the human mind, which is confused
In the relationship between the human demand for meaning and the world's silence
In language, which cannot describe reality
quiz.explanation: The absurd is a confrontation or divorce between two terms; remove either the questioning human or the silent world, and it disappears.

quiz.question: Camus concludes that recognising the absurd logically requires suicide.
quiz.explanation: He rejects suicide because it abolishes the absurd instead of living with it; his answer is revolt, freedom and passion.

quiz.question: What does Camus mean by philosophical suicide?
options: Abandoning philosophy for a practical career
Leaping from the absurd into a hope or faith that the mind cannot justify
Killing oneself for philosophical reasons
Refusing to read other philosophers
quiz.explanation: Thinkers like Kierkegaard see the absurd but then escape it by a leap of faith, sacrificing lucidity.

quiz.question: Why is the walk back down the hill the key moment for Sisyphus?
options: Because it is when he plans his escape
Because the gods reduce his punishment then
Because he finally finds the meaning of the boulder
Because it is the hour of consciousness, when he lucidly faces his fate and makes it his own
quiz.explanation: In that pause Sisyphus is fully aware of his condition; his lucidity and scorn make the fate his own.

quiz.question: A nurse during an epidemic says, “I don't think I'm a hero. I'm just doing my job because people are sick.” Which Camus character does she most resemble?
options: Doctor Rieux in *The Plague*
Meursault in *The Stranger*
Don Juan in *The Myth of Sisyphus*
Caligula
quiz.explanation: Rieux fights the plague without illusions or heroics, out of decency and solidarity.

quiz.question: In *The Stranger*, Meursault's failure to weep at his mother's funeral weighs heavily in his trial.
quiz.explanation: The prosecution dwells on his apparent coldness, and Camus later said that a man who does not weep at his mother's funeral risks being condemned to death.

quiz.question: What does Camus's formula “I rebel, therefore we exist” express?
options: That rebellion proves the existence of God
That individuals exist only through political parties
That in saying no to injustice the rebel affirms a value shared by all human beings
That revolution justifies any means
quiz.explanation: The rebel's refusal implies a limit and a common human dignity, so rebellion reveals solidarity.

quiz.question: What ended the friendship between Camus and Sartre in 1952?
options: A dispute over who would win the Nobel Prize
A hostile review of *The Rebel* in Sartre's journal and the bitter public exchange that followed
Camus's conversion to Christianity
Sartre's criticism of *The Stranger*
quiz.explanation: Francis Jeanson's review in *Les Temps modernes*, Camus's reply and Sartre's cutting response ended the friendship, largely over Communism and revolutionary violence.

quiz.question: Camus happily accepted being called an existentialist.
quiz.explanation: He repeatedly rejected the label, distancing himself from Sartre's philosophy.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest criticism of applying “imagine Sisyphus happy” to an exploited worker?
options: Workers never ask about meaning
Camus never wrote about work
Sisyphus was a real historical king
Unlike Sisyphus, workers can often change their situation, so acceptance could become a false consolation that excuses injustice
quiz.explanation: Camus's own idea of revolt includes saying no to unnecessary suffering imposed by others; the other options are false.

goDeeper.body:
Three debates take Camus further. First, **is his argument valid?** Thomas Nagel's essay “The Absurd” (1971) agrees that life can seem absurd, but locates the source differently: we are capable of stepping back and viewing our lives from a cosmic perspective, from which our serious concerns look arbitrary, while still being unable to stop taking them seriously. For Nagel the right response is irony, not Camus's heroic defiance, which he finds a bit melodramatic. Compare the two and ask whose diagnosis is more accurate.

Second, **Camus and Algeria.** Conor Cruise O'Brien's short critical study argued that Camus's fiction quietly excludes Arab Algerians and that his politics reflected the limits of a settler. Edward Said, in *Culture and Imperialism* (1993), read *The Stranger* and *The Plague* as part of the cultural geography of French colonialism. Defenders reply that Camus's journalism exposed colonial misery long before it was fashionable, and that his refusal to justify terrorism by anyone was principled. Kamel Daoud's novel *The Meursault Investigation* adds a literary reply from the other side.

Third, **the ethics of limits.** *The Rebel* argued that revolutions turn murderous when they claim history as their judge. This idea fed into later criticisms of utopian politics, and Camus's insistence on refusing to be either victims or executioners (the title of a 1946 series of his articles in *Combat*) connects him to Arendt's analysis of totalitarianism, which you will meet tomorrow (Day 80). Was Camus naive about how injustice can be ended without violence, or wise about what violence does to those who use it?

readings.note: A balanced account of the most famous philosophical feud of the century.

questions: Is Camus right that we cannot know whether life has an ultimate meaning, or is that already a philosophical leap of its own?
Can happiness exist without hope? What would that happiness be like?
Is it ever justified to kill for a better future? How would Camus and Sartre each answer?
